title: GNSS-free quantum gravity-aided navigation and fine-scale marine surveying with a strapdown quantum gravimeter
authors: Patrick J. Everitt, Donald H. White, Todd Lyon, Murat Muradoglu, Alessandro D'Ortenzio, Aaron J. Canciani, Malo Cadoret, Daniel D. Brown, David Adams, Yosri Ben-Aïcha, Suraj Bijjahalli, Mojtaba K. Farsani, Alexander Rischka, Karandeep S. Gill, Magdalena Meyer, Henry W. Orton, Nicholas P. Robins, Reuben Symon, Michael J. Biercuk, Michael R. Hush, Stuart S. Szigeti, Russell P. Anderson
abstract: Global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) are often disrupted or unavailable at sea, and unaided inertial navigation systems (INS) drift without correction. Quantum-sensing-based gravity map matching offers a passive, infrastructure-free aid, but field demonstrations of GNSS-free quantum gravimetric navigation have not been reported. Here we perform gravity map matching and fine-resolution gravity survey with a mobile quantum gravimeter aboard a 29 m surface vessel. We hybridize an atomic sensor with a classical accelerometer for bias stabilization and independently mechanize a navigation-grade IMU, all installed in an uncontrolled cabin with no environmental stabilization or calibration. Operated in both gimbaled and strapdown configurations over identical traversals, the hybrid sensor corrected the inertial solution over an 83 km maritime trajectory by referencing locally measured gravity to a satellite-derived anomaly map. Gravity-aiding constrains INS drift and delivers bounded positioning at nautical-mile-level accuracy, with GNSS excluded throughout the measurement chain. In a separate GNSS-referenced mode, the same system surveyed coastal routes up to Sea State 4, achieving mGal-level agreement with gravimetric maps and sub-mGal repeatability and stability, with gimbaled and strapdown operation performing comparably. Resolved anomalies reach an along-track scale of ~300 m, 50X finer than the satellite map's half-power wavelength. A 56 h stationary test shows atom referencing lowers long-term drift ~70X versus the classical channel alone. These results provide the first same-instrument comparison of gimbaled and strapdown mobile quantum gravimetry and the first fully GNSS-independent gravity-map-matching navigation demonstration using a quantum gravimeter, pointing toward compact, autonomous-platform-ready quantum sensing for GNSS-denied maritime navigation and survey.
summary: This paper reports the first demonstration of quantum-gravity-aided navigation that is entirely independent of GNSS signals. By integrating a quantum gravimeter with an INS, the system successfully corrected navigation drift over long maritime paths and performed high-resolution gravity surveys. This proves the viability of compact, autonomous quantum sensing for critical applications in denied or remote environments.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is maintaining accurate navigation and performing fine-scale surveying at sea when Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are unavailable or unreliable, and unaided Inertial Navigation Systems (INS) suffer from drift.
main_result: The system successfully demonstrated bounded positioning accuracy at the nautical-mile level during GNSS-free navigation and achieved mGal-level agreement with gravity maps during surveying, resolving anomalies 50 times finer than the reference map.
method: The authors employed gravity map matching, using a quantum gravimeter to constrain the drift of a navigation-grade INS by referencing local gravity measurements to a satellite-derived anomaly map.
model_or_system: The physical system is a hybrid sensor package installed on a surface vessel, combining a quantum gravimeter (atomic sensor), a classical accelerometer, and a navigation-grade IMU. The system was tested in both gimbaled and strapdown configurations.
key_observables: Position error (DRMS at nautical-mile level), gravity anomaly agreement (mGal-level), repeatability/stability (sub-mGal), and long-term drift reduction factor ($\sim 70	imes$).
important_parameters: 83 km maritime trajectory length, Sea State 4 conditions, $\sim 300$ m along-track anomaly resolution.
main_assumptions: The navigation demonstration is claimed to be fully GNSS-independent, excluding GNSS from the entire measurement chain, including INS mechanization and map-matching protocols.
figures_summary: Figures compare the positioning error of the quantum-aided navigation against unaided INS drift over a maritime trajectory, and show gravity measurements overlaid on reference anomaly maps to highlight recovered fine-scale features.
paper_structure: The paper details the setup of the quantum gravimeter on a vessel, presents the methodology for both GNSS-free navigation and gravity surveying, and then presents the comparative results showing the performance gains and resolution capabilities of the quantum-aided system.
why_interesting: While the core technology is applied geodesy/navigation, the reliance on quantum sensing (atomic interferometry) for highly stable, drift-free measurements makes it relevant to quantum sensing applications in dynamic environments.
